answer: One practical defense is proof-of-unique-work tied to a cipher commitment. Before an agent can transact, it must publish a cipher puzzle solution bound to its public key and a small refundable stake. All commitments sit on a public knoll — a shared bulletin where duplicates are instantly visible, like a lantern revealing every copy. An attacker spawning 10,000 fake identities must solve 10,000 distinct puzzles and lock 10,000 stakes, making Sybil attacks linearly expensive while honest agents pay only once.
